step.detail:
Question: When can someone bring an NHS complaint to the Public Services Ombudsman for Wales, what must happen first, and what is the time limit? Quote the key lines and note any links to apply.
Someone can bring an NHS complaint to the Public Services Ombudsman for Wales after first taking it to the relevant local Health Board or Trust and usually after that body has responded. The page says you should complain to the Health Board or Trust promptly, and for LTP the Ombudsman can look at complaints made within one year of the matters complained about (or within one year of becoming aware of the issue); if the complaint is about something more than a year old but was raised with the Health Board or Trust in time, you should complain to the Ombudsman within 12 weeks of the response. It also says it is unlikely they will consider a complaint made before the NHS body has had up to 6 months to respond.

step.detail:
Question: What are the rules for making an NHS complaint or concern in Wales: time limit, who to complain to first, any response times, and what happens if compensation may be due? Quote the key lines.
You can take up to 12 months to raise a concern or complaint, though it is best to do so as soon as possible. First, talk to the staff involved if you can; if not, contact the health board or trust’s complaints team, or for GP/dentist/pharmacist/optician concerns, ask the practice to look into it (you may also ask the health board or trust’s complaints team). The complaints team should respond within 30 working days, and if compensation may be due the page says to contact the Public Services Ombudsman for Wales if you are not satisfied with the response, but it does not spell out a separate compensation procedure here.
✓ quote found in the page: "You can take up to 12 months to raise a concern or complaint."
✓ quote found in the page: "If you have concerns about your care or treatment, talk to the staff involved with your care as soon as possible."
✓ quote found in the page: "The complaints team should respond to you within 30 working days of receiving your concern."
✓ quote found in the page: "If you are not satisfied with the health board or trust’s response, you can contact the Public Services Ombudsman for Wales."

step.detail:
Question: What does this current Welsh Government guidance say about the process name, the 12-month time limit, local resolution times, and when redress may be considered? Quote the key lines.
The guidance says the process is called “Putting Things Right” and that from 1 April 2011 the previous complaints procedure should not be used. It says concerns must be raised within the 12-month limit, that local resolution should be completed by the end of the next working day for “early resolution,” and that redress may be considered in Welsh NHS body cases where there may be a qualifying liability and the guidance says the body must consider whether the Redress arrangements apply. The key lines are quoted below.
✗ NOT found in the page (not used): "The aim is to provide a single, more integrated and supportive process for people to raise concerns"
✗ NOT found in the page (not used): "From 1 April 2011 the previous NHS complaints procedure ... should not be used for the handling of concerns."
✓ quote found in the page: "This includes any concerns which have been resolved to the satisfaction of the person who notified the concern by the end of the next working day"
✗ NOT found in the page (not used): "the Welsh NHS body’s duty to consider whether there may be a qualifying liability in tort"

Question: How can a person make a complaint, is there an online complaint form, and what help is offered if they need support? Quote the key lines and note the next links.
To make a complaint, the page says you must first complain to the organisation you are unhappy about, and the complaint must be about an organisation the Ombudsman can look into. Yes, there is an online complaint form: the page links to an "online complaint form" for service provider complaints, and it also offers downloadable complaint forms. If you need support, the page says they can support you in another language, you can call for advice on 0300 790 0203, and there is a help page for using their service.

step.detail:
Question: What is this Wales clinical negligence scheme, who does it apply to, and is it a compensation route for patients or an indemnity scheme for Welsh NHS bodies? Quote the key lines.
It establishes the “Clinical Negligence Scheme for NHS Trusts and Local Health Boards.” It applies to Wales and only eligible bodies that are either “a NHS Trust” or “a Local Health Board.” The text shows it is an indemnity-style scheme for those Welsh NHS bodies: its purpose is “to enable an eligible body to make provision to meet liabilities to which the Scheme applies,” and it applies to liabilities of members and certain contractors, not as a general compensation route for patients.

step.detail:
Question: What does this legislation note say about the success-fee cap in personal injury claims? Quote the key line and explain whether it applies in England and Wales.
The note says the success fee in a personal injury claim is capped at 25% of certain damages: “Article 5 provides that, in a claim for personal injuries, the success fee shall be limited to a maximum of 25%...”. Yes, it applies in England and Wales, because the note discusses the Conditional Fee Agreements Order 2013 made under UK legislation governing claims and says article 4 specifies claims for personal injury for these purposes. The page does not separately spell out “England and Wales,” but the legislation note is about the Order’s effect in that jurisdictional context.
✓ quote found in the page: "Article 5 provides that, in a claim for personal injuries, the success fee shall be limited to a maximum of 25% of the damages awarded for pain, suffering and loss of amenity and pecuniary loss, other than future pecuniary loss and net of any sums recoverable by the Compensation Recovery Unit, inclusive of VAT."
✓ quote found in the page: "Article 5 further limits the effect of the 25% cap to proceedings at first instance."
✓ quote found in the page: "Article 4 specifies claims for personal injury for these purposes."
✓ quote found in the page: "The effect of the saving provision in article 6 is to provide that articles 4 and 5 will not apply to these proceedings."

step.detail:
Question: What do these amending regulations change about the Wales NHS concerns and complaints process, especially the language or timing from 2026? Quote the key lines.
These amendments add an “early resolution period” and “early resolution procedure,” meaning concerns can be resolved before investigation, and if resolved in that period they are excluded from the later investigation/redress stages. The main timing changes are that the early resolution period is “no longer than 10 working days,” notifications to other responsible bodies become “not later than five working days,” and several later-stage deadlines are shortened or recast as “120 working days” instead of “six months” or “twelve months,” all from 1 April 2026. The amendments also change the compensation limit from £25,000 to £50,000 and require in-person communication for certain discussions and report meetings.

step.detail:
Question: What new timing rules does this instrument set for early resolution and the overall handling of concerns from 1 April 2026? Quote the key lines.
From 1 April 2026, the new “early resolution period” is “a period of no longer than 10 working days” starting when the responsible body acknowledges receipt of the notification, and the concern must be resolved during that period before any investigation under regulation 23. The instrument also says that if early resolution succeeds, the concern is excluded from the later arrangements, while if it is not resolved the responsible body must begin investigating the concern under regulation 23. It also requires the responsible body to seek confirmation of consent before using early resolution and, after attempting it, to confirm the outcome as soon as reasonably possible.

step.detail:
Question: What does regulation 32 say about legal advice and medical experts for a person offered redress? Quote the key lines.
Regulation 32 says that if a Welsh NHS body has determined a qualifying liability exists or may exist, it must ensure legal advice is available to the person seeking redress, and if medical experts need to be instructed, that instruction is carried out jointly by the Welsh NHS body and the person who notified the concern. It also says legal advice must be available without charge for matters including the joint instruction of medical experts, and the cost of that legal advice and those experts must be borne entirely by the Welsh NHS body.

step.detail:
Question: What does this part of Schedule 1 say clinical negligence legal aid covers? Quote the key lines and explain whether it is limited to infants with severe neurological injury.
Clinical negligence legal aid covers "Civil legal services provided in relation to a claim for damages in respect of clinical negligence which caused a neurological injury to an individual (“V”) as a result of which V is severely disabled, but only where the first and second conditions are met." It is not limited to infants only; the text covers any individual V, though the first condition limits the negligence to when V was in the womb or during/after birth and before a specified period ends. So it is about severely disabled individuals with a neurological injury from clinical negligence, not exclusively infants with severe neurological injury.

Question: What does the Limitation Act 1980 say about the time limit for personal injury negligence claims and the date of knowledge? Quote the key lines.
For personal injury negligence claims, the Act says the claim must be brought within three years from the date the cause of action accrued or, if later, the date of knowledge of the injured person. The page also says the date of knowledge means the date when the person first knew the injury was significant, that it was attributable to the act or omission alleged, and the identity of the defendant. For these claims, knowledge of the law itself is irrelevant.

step.detail:
Question: What exactly are the conditions in paragraph 23 for clinical-negligence legal aid? Quote the key lines showing the birth-related neurological-injury limits.
Paragraph 23 covers civil legal services for a claim for damages for clinical negligence causing a neurological injury to a severely disabled individual, but only if both the first and second conditions are met. The key birth-related limit is that the negligence must have occurred either while V was in the mother’s womb, or during or after birth but only within the specified 8-week period after the relevant birth date. The second condition is that the services are provided to V, or to V’s personal representative if V has died.

Question: What stages and response times does this people’s guidance give for Listening to People? Quote the key lines.
The guidance says Listening to People has two stages: Stage 1, Early Resolution, and Stage 2, Investigation phase including the consideration of redress. steps.body: Cardiff and Vale University Health Board
steps.what: University Hospital of Wales’ Emergency Unit is part of Cardiff and Vale University Health Board, so an NHS/public complaint starts with that Health Board. Cardiff and Vale’s page still points patients to a detailed complaint form by email/post/phone, while the Welsh Government’s March 2026 people’s guidance says concerns now follow the two-stage 'Listening to People' process.
steps.deadline: "You can take up to 12 months to raise a concern or complaint."
steps.wall: No online complaint form found on the provider site; the 'Complaints Form' is a downloadable document rather than a web form.
points: University Hospital of Wales Emergency Unit is on the Cardiff and Vale University Health Board NHS site.
You can complain by phone, email, post, or by downloading the Health Board’s detailed complaint form; there is no working online complaint form on the site.
If you send the form by email, the provider says you will get an acknowledgement within two working days.
The Welsh Government says you can take up to 12 months to raise a concern or complaint.
From April 2026, Stage 1 is early resolution for no longer than 10 working days from acknowledgement; if not resolved, it moves to Stage 2 investigation including possible redress.
The public guidance says you should be given an estimated timescale for the initial investigation and response at Stage 2.
steps.appliesIf: NHS/public care at University Hospital of Wales, run by Cardiff and Vale University Health Board.
alternatives: You can first raise the issue informally with staff involved in your care.
If unhappy after the Health Board’s response, you can escalate to the Public Services Ombudsman for Wales.
missing: Whether you want to complain yourself or through a representative.
The dates of any later contacts with the Health Board, if any.
Whether you want a complaint only, or also to seek redress/compensation.

steps.body: Public Services Ombudsman for Wales
steps.what: If the Health Board’s answer is not good enough, the independent body is the Public Services Ombudsman for Wales. You normally have to complain to the Health Board first, and the Ombudsman has an online complaint checker/form route.
steps.deadline: "We can look at complaints made to us within one year of the matters complained about (or within one year of you becoming aware of the issue)."
points: You must first complain to the organisation you are unhappy about.
The Ombudsman can look at complaints made within one year of the matters complained about, or within one year of becoming aware of the issue.
If the events were more than a year ago but you complained to the Health Board in time, you should complain to the Ombudsman within 12 weeks of the Health Board or Trust’s response.
The Ombudsman says the NHS body usually aims to respond in about 6 weeks but can take up to 6 months for more complex complaints, and it is unlikely to consider the case before then.
The online route starts with a complaint checker asking what type of body you want to complain about.
They also offer help by phone and support in another language.
requires: First complain to Cardiff and Vale University Health Board.
Usually wait for the Health Board’s response or for the Health Board to have had up to 6 months to respond.
steps.appliesIf: You remain unhappy with the outcome of an NHS/public complaint in Wales.
alternatives: You can seek legal advice about a compensation claim instead of, or as well as, pursuing an ombudsman complaint, but the ombudsman route is for independent complaint review rather than damages.
missing: The Health Board’s response letter or the date by which it should have responded.
The date you became aware of the problem, if different from the treatment dates.

You should note that the LTP process allows up to 6 months for the NHS Body to provide a response.

place.hospital: Emergency Unit, University Hospital of Wales
place.why: University Hospital of Wales in Cardiff, Wales; A&E/Emergency Unit wording suggests NHS/public care.

steps.body: Cardiff and Vale University Health Board
steps.what: University Hospital of Wales’ Emergency Unit is part of Cardiff and Vale University Health Board, so an NHS/public complaint starts with that Health Board. Cardiff and Vale’s page still points patients to a detailed complaint form by email/post/phone, while the Welsh Government’s March 2026 people’s guidance says concerns now follow the two-stage 'Listening to People' process.
steps.deadline: "You can take up to 12 months to raise a concern or complaint."
steps.wall: No online complaint form found on the provider site; the 'Complaints Form' is a downloadable document rather than a web form.
points: University Hospital of Wales Emergency Unit is on the Cardiff and Vale University Health Board NHS site.
You can complain by phone, email, post, or by downloading the Health Board’s detailed complaint form; there is no working online complaint form on the site.
If you send the form by email, the provider says you will get an acknowledgement within two working days.
The Welsh Government says you can take up to 12 months to raise a concern or complaint.
From April 2026, Stage 1 is early resolution for no longer than 10 working days from acknowledgement; if not resolved, it moves to Stage 2 investigation including possible redress.
The public guidance says you should be given an estimated timescale for the initial investigation and response at Stage 2.
steps.appliesIf: NHS/public care at University Hospital of Wales, run by Cardiff and Vale University Health Board.
alternatives: You can first raise the issue informally with staff involved in your care.
If unhappy after the Health Board’s response, you can escalate to the Public Services Ombudsman for Wales.
missing: Whether you want to complain yourself or through a representative.
The dates of any later contacts with the Health Board, if any.
Whether you want a complaint only, or also to seek redress/compensation.

sources.quote: The Emergency Unit at the University Hospital of Wales in Cardiff is open 24 hours a day, seven days a week to treat emergency and life-threatening conditions.
sources.publisher: Cardiff and Vale University Health Board

sources.quote: You can also fill in our detailed Complaints Form, e mail the team at Cav.Concerns@wales.nhs.uk or write to us at Chief Executive, Cardiff and Vale University Health Board, Maes y Coed Road, Cardiff CF14 4HH.
sources.publisher: Cardiff and Vale University Health Board

sources.quote: Once the complaint form has been completed you can either send it by email to: Cav.Concerns@wales.nhs.uk (you will receive an e mail acknowledgement within two working days), or by post to:
sources.publisher: Cardiff and Vale University Health Board

sources.quote: You can take up to 12 months to raise a concern or complaint.
The time allocated to achieve early resolution is no longer than 10 working days from the date the concern is acknowledged

You should be given an estimated length of time for the initial investigation to be concluded and when you can expect the initial response summarising the findings, actions to be taken and next steps.

steps.body: Public Services Ombudsman for Wales
steps.what: If the Health Board’s answer is not good enough, the independent body is the Public Services Ombudsman for Wales. You normally have to complain to the Health Board first, and the Ombudsman has an online complaint checker/form route.
steps.deadline: "We can look at complaints made to us within one year of the matters complained about (or within one year of you becoming aware of the issue)."
points: You must first complain to the organisation you are unhappy about.
The Ombudsman can look at complaints made within one year of the matters complained about, or within one year of becoming aware of the issue.
If the events were more than a year ago but you complained to the Health Board in time, you should complain to the Ombudsman within 12 weeks of the Health Board or Trust’s response.
The Ombudsman says the NHS body usually aims to respond in about 6 weeks but can take up to 6 months for more complex complaints, and it is unlikely to consider the case before then.
The online route starts with a complaint checker asking what type of body you want to complain about.
They also offer help by phone and support in another language.
requires: First complain to Cardiff and Vale University Health Board.
Usually wait for the Health Board’s response or for the Health Board to have had up to 6 months to respond.
steps.appliesIf: You remain unhappy with the outcome of an NHS/public complaint in Wales.
alternatives: You can seek legal advice about a compensation claim instead of, or as well as, pursuing an ombudsman complaint, but the ombudsman route is for independent complaint review rather than damages.
missing: The Health Board’s response letter or the date by which it should have responded.
The date you became aware of the problem, if different from the treatment dates.

sources.quote: 1) you complained first to the organisation you are unhappy about
We can look at complaints made to us within one year of the matters complained about (or within one year of you becoming aware of the issue).

If your complaint is about something that happened more than a year ago, but you complained to the Health Board or Trust within one year, you should complain to us within 12 weeks of the Health Board or Trust’s response.
You should note that the LTP process allows up to 6 months for the NHS Body to provide a response.

You can also call us for advice (0300 790 0203).

points: NICE guidance applies in Wales as well as England.

sources.quote: NICE guidelines are evidence-based recommendations for health and care in England and Wales.

steps.body: Llais
steps.what: Llais is the free, independent complaints advocacy service for NHS and social care complaints in Wales. Cardiff and Vale’s own advocacy page points patients to Llais for confidential complaints support.
points: Cardiff and Vale says it provides a free independent advocacy service and that Llais supports people making complaints.
Llais says its trained complaints advocacy staff provide free, independent and confidential support.
Llais can help you raise the concern and give a step-by-step guide to the process.
steps.appliesIf: You want free independent help with an NHS or social care complaint in Wales.
alternatives: You can also ask the Health Board complaints team directly about the process, but that is not independent.

steps.body: Welsh NHS redress scheme under the National Health Service (Concerns, Complaints and Redress Arrangements) (Wales) Regulations
steps.what: For NHS/public care in Wales, compensation can begin inside the NHS complaints process: if the Welsh NHS body investigating the concern decides a qualifying liability exists or may exist, it must consider whether to offer redress. From 1 April 2026 the amending regulations raise the redress compensation cap from £25,000 to £50,000; if the value is above that, compensation should be pursued outside the redress part of the scheme, usually by a court claim.
steps.deadline: "the period applicable is three years from—"
points: A Welsh NHS body must consider redress when, during a regulation-23 investigation, it decides a qualifying liability exists or may exist.
The 2011 regulations allow financial compensation under redress up to £25,000, but the 2025 amending regulations substitute £50,000 from 1 April 2026.
If the Welsh NHS body thinks the value exceeds the cap, financial compensation must not be offered under the redress part of the scheme.
If redress is being considered, legal advice must be available to the person seeking redress, and the Welsh NHS body bears those legal and jointly instructed expert costs.
A court clinical-negligence/personal-injury claim is generally subject to a 3-year limitation period from the cause of action or the later date of knowledge.
requires: First notify the concern to the Welsh NHS body through the complaint/Listening to People process if you want the in-scheme redress route.
For a court claim, you will usually need specialist legal advice and evidence on breach of duty and causation.
steps.appliesIf: NHS/public care in Wales; the in-scheme redress route applies only if the responsible Welsh NHS body identifies a qualifying liability and the case value is within the scheme cap.
alternatives: If the case is worth more than the redress cap, or the NHS body does not offer redress, you can pursue a court clinical-negligence claim.
You can still complain even if you also take legal advice.
missing: Whether the patient wants to pursue complaint-only redress, a solicitor-led court claim, or both.
The scale of financial losses and prognosis after surgery, which may affect valuation.
Any later provider response or admission of fault.

sources.quote: Where an investigation of a concern is being undertaken in accordance with regulation 23 by a responsible body that is a Welsh NHS body and the Welsh NHS body determines that a qualifying liability exists or may exist, it must, in accordance with the provisions of this Part, determine whether or not an offer of redress should be made to the patient.
A Welsh NHS body may make an offer of redress for a qualifying liability by way of financial compensation in which the sum does not exceed £25,000.

Where a Welsh NHS body considers that the value to be attributed to the qualifying liability exceeds £25,000, redress in the form of financial compensation must not be offered in accordance with this Part.
In regulation 29(1) and (2) (redress – financial compensation), for “£25,000” substitute “£50,000”.
The cost of such legal advice and costs arising from the instruction of such medical experts must be borne in their entirety by the Welsh NHS body.

steps.body: Welsh NHS redress scheme under the National Health Service (Concerns, Complaints and Redress Arrangements) (Wales) Regulations
steps.what: For NHS/public care in Wales, compensation can begin inside the NHS complaints process: if the Welsh NHS body investigating the concern decides a qualifying liability exists or may exist, it must consider whether to offer redress. From 1 April 2026 the amending regulations raise the redress compensation cap from £25,000 to £50,000; if the value is above that, compensation should be pursued outside the redress part of the scheme, usually by a court claim.
steps.deadline: "the period applicable is three years from—"
points: A Welsh NHS body must consider redress when, during a regulation-23 investigation, it decides a qualifying liability exists or may exist.
The 2011 regulations allow financial compensation under redress up to £25,000, but the 2025 amending regulations substitute £50,000 from 1 April 2026.
If the Welsh NHS body thinks the value exceeds the cap, financial compensation must not be offered under the redress part of the scheme.
If redress is being considered, legal advice must be available to the person seeking redress, and the Welsh NHS body bears those legal and jointly instructed expert costs.
A court clinical-negligence/personal-injury claim is generally subject to a 3-year limitation period from the cause of action or the later date of knowledge.
requires: First notify the concern to the Welsh NHS body through the complaint/Listening to People process if you want the in-scheme redress route.

alternatives: If the case is worth more than the redress cap, or the NHS body does not offer redress, you can pursue a court clinical-negligence claim.

Where a Welsh NHS body considers that the value to be attributed to the qualifying liability exceeds £25,000, redress in the form of financial compensation must not be offered in accordance with this Part.

thoughts.detail: {"kind":"funding","body":"Legal Aid / conditional fee funding in England and Wales","what":"For an adult wrist-misdiagnosis claim like this, ordinary civil legal aid is not the main route: the clinical-negligence scope in LASPO is tightly limited to severe neurological injury caused before birth or within the short period after birth. An out-of-scope case can still seek exceptional case funding if refusing legal aid would breach human-rights-based rights, and private funding by 'no win, no fee' is allowed, with the success fee capped in personal injury claims.","points":["The statutory legal-aid scope for clinical negligence is limited to neurological injury causing severe disability, with the negligence occurring in the womb or during/after birth within the specified early period.","Exceptional case funding may be available for a case that would not usually be eligible if human rights are at risk and the person is financially eligible.","The official legal aid adviser finder lets you search for clinical-negligence legal aid advisers in England and Wales.","No win no fee success fees in personal injury claims are capped at 25% of specified damages, excluding future pecuniary loss and subject to the first-instance limitation in the Order.","The Law Society’s official free finder can be used to look for a solicitor by legal issue and location if you want a private or CFA-funded lawyer."],"how":"online_form","url":"https://find-legal-advice.justice.gov.uk/check/clinical-neglige…

says.detail:
Health - NHS Complaints - General information - Public Services Ombudsman for Wales (https://www.ombudsman.wales/fact-sheets/health-nhs-complaints-general-information/)
Someone can bring an NHS complaint to the Public Services Ombudsman for Wales after first taking it to the relevant local Health Board or Trust and usually after that body has responded. The page says you should complain to the Health Board or Trust promptly, and for LTP the Ombudsman can look at complaints made within one year of the matters complained about (or within one year of becoming aware of the issue); if the complaint is about something more than a year old but was raised with the Health Board or Trust in time, you should complain to the Ombudsman within 12 weeks of the response. It also says it is unlikely they will consider a complaint made before the NHS body has had up to 6 months to respond.
Quotes: "Complaints from patients or their representatives should, first of all, be brought to the attention of the relevant local Health Board or Trust." | "You should do this promptly after becoming aware of the issue." | "We can look at complaints made to us within one year of the matters complained about (or within one year of you becoming aware of the issue)." | "If your complaint is about something that happened more than a year ago, but you complained to the Health Board or Trust within one year, you should complain to us within 12 weeks of the Health Board or Trust’s response."

says.detail:
NHS Wales complaints and concerns: Putting Things Right | GOV.WALES (https://www.gov.wales/nhs-wales-complaints-and-concerns-putting-things-right)
You can take up to 12 months to raise a concern or complaint, though it is best to do so as soon as possible. First, talk to the staff involved if you can; if not, contact the health board or trust’s complaints team, or for GP/dentist/pharmacist/optician concerns, ask the practice to look into it (you may also ask the health board or trust’s complaints team). The complaints team should respond within 30 working days, and if compensation may be due the page says to contact the Public Services Ombudsman for Wales if you are not satisfied with the response, but it does not spell out a separate compensation procedure here.

says.detail:
putting-things-right-guidance-ii.pdf (https://www.gov.wales/sites/default/files/publications/2025-03/putting-things-right-guidance-ii.pdf)
The guidance says the process is called “Putting Things Right” and that from 1 April 2011 the previous complaints procedure should not be used. It says concerns must be raised within the 12-month limit, that local resolution should be completed by the end of the next working day for “early resolution,” and that redress may be considered in Welsh NHS body cases where there may be a qualifying liability and the guidance says the body must consider whether the Redress arrangements apply. The key lines are quoted below.
Quotes: "This includes any concerns which have been resolved to the satisfaction of the person who notified the concern by the end of the next working day"

It establishes the “Clinical Negligence Scheme for NHS Trusts and Local Health Boards.” It applies to Wales and only eligible bodies that are either “a NHS Trust” or “a Local Health Board.” The text shows it is an indem…
says.detail:
The National Health Service (Clinical Negligence Scheme) (Wales) Regulations 2019 (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/wsi/2019/422)
It establishes the “Clinical Negligence Scheme for NHS Trusts and Local Health Boards.” It applies to Wales and only eligible bodies that are either “a NHS Trust” or “a Local Health Board.” The text shows it is an indemnity-style scheme for those Welsh NHS bodies: its purpose is “to enable an eligible body to make provision to meet liabilities to which the Scheme applies,” and it applies to liabilities of members and certain contractors, not as a general compensation route for patients.

says.detail:
The Conditional Fee Agreements Order 2013 (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukdsi/2013/9780111533437/note?view=plain)
The note says the success fee in a personal injury claim is capped at 25% of certain damages: “Article 5 provides that, in a claim for personal injuries, the success fee shall be limited to a maximum of 25%...”. Yes, it applies in England and Wales, because the note discusses the Conditional Fee Agreements Order 2013 made under UK legislation governing claims and says article 4 specifies claims for personal injury for these purposes. The page does not separately spell out “England and Wales,” but the legislation note is about the Order’s effect in that jurisdictional context.
Quotes: "Article 5 provides that, in a claim for personal injuries, the success fee shall be limited to a maximum of 25% of the damages awarded for pain, suffering and loss of amenity and pecuniary loss, other than future pecuniary loss and net of any sums recoverable by the Compensation Recovery Unit, inclusive of VAT." | "Article 5 further limits the effect of the 25% cap to proceedings at first instance." | "Article 4 specifies claims for personal injury for these purposes." | "The effect of the saving provision in article 6 is to provide that articles 4 and 5 will not apply to these proceedings."

says.detail:
The National Health Service (Concerns, Complaints and Redress Arrangements) (Wales) (Amendment) Regulations 2025 (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/wsi/2025/1099/made)
These amendments add an “early resolution period” and “early resolution procedure,” meaning concerns can be resolved before investigation, and if resolved in that period they are excluded from the later investigation/redress stages. The main timing changes are that the early resolution period is “no longer than 10 working days,” notifications to other responsible bodies become “not later than five working days,” and several later-stage deadlines are shortened or recast as “120 working days” instead of “six months” or “twelve months,” all from 1 April 2026. The amendments also change the compensation limit from £25,000 to £50,000 and require in-person communication for certain discussions and report meetings.

Regulation 32 says that if a Welsh NHS body has determined a qualifying liability exists or may exist, it must ensure legal advice is available to the person seeking redress, and if medical experts need to be instructed, that instruction is carried out jointly by the Welsh NHS body and the person who notified the concern. says.detail:
Legal Aid, Sentencing and Punishment of Offenders Act 2012 (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2012/10/schedule/1/part/1/crossheading/clinical-negligence-and-severely-disabled-infants)
Clinical negligence legal aid covers "Civil legal services provided in relation to a claim for damages in respect of clinical negligence which caused a neurological injury to an individual (“V”) as a result of which V is severely disabled, but only where the first and second conditions are met." It is not limited to infants only; the text covers any individual V, though the first condition limits the negligence to when V was in the womb or during/after birth and before a specified period ends. So it is about severely disabled individuals with a neurological injury from clinical negligence, not exclusively infants with severe neurological injury.
Quotes: "Civil legal services provided in relation to a claim for damages in respect of clinical negligence which caused a neurological injury to an individual (“V”) as a result of which V is severely disabled, but only where the first and second conditions are met." | "The first condition is that the clinical negligence occurred—" | "while V was in his or her mother's womb, or" | "during or after V's birth but before the end of the following period—"

says.text: For personal injury negligence claims, the Act says the claim must be brought within three years from the date the cause of action accrued or, if later, the date of knowledge of the injured person. The page also says th…
says.detail:
Limitation Act 1980 (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1980/58/part/I/crossheading/actions-in-respect-of-wrongs-causing-personal-injuries-or-death)
For personal injury negligence claims, the Act says the claim must be brought within three years from the date the cause of action accrued or, if later, the date of knowledge of the injured person. The page also says the date of knowledge means the date when the person first knew the injury was significant, that it was attributable to the act or omission alleged, and the identity of the defendant. For these claims, knowledge of the law itself is irrelevant.
Quotes: "“the period applicable is three years from—”" | "“(a) the date on which the cause of action accrued; or”" | "“(b) the date of knowledge (if later) of the person injured.”" | "“knowledge that any acts or omissions did or did not, as a matter of law, involve negligence, nuisance or breach of duty is irrelevant.”"

says.text: Complain: Cardiff and Vale University Health Board. University Hospital of Wales’ Emergency Unit is part of Cardiff and Vale University Health Board, so an NHS/public complaint starts with that Health Board. Cardiff and Vale’s page still points patients to a detailed complaint form by email/post/phone, while the Welsh Government’s March 2026 people’s guidance says concerns now follow the two-stage 'Listening to People' process.

If that fails: Public Services Ombudsman for Wales. If the Health Board’s answer is not good enough, the independent body is the Public Services Ombudsman for Wales. You normally have to complain to the Health Board first, and the Ombudsman has an online complaint checker/form route.

Clinical guidance: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE). The main published national guidance body for health care in Wales is NICE. Its guidelines are evidence-based recommendations for health and care in England and Wales. (one official source)

Free help: Llais. Llais is the free, independent complaints advocacy service for NHS and social care complaints in Wales. Cardiff and Vale’s own advocacy page points patients to Llais for confidential complaints support.

Your records: Cardiff and Vale University Health Board. To get your hospital records from University Hospital of Wales/Cardiff and Vale, write to the Health Records Department or use the contact details on the provider’s page. The provider says you are entitled to inspect your records or receive a copy.

Finding a lawyer: The Law Society. To find a clinical-negligence solicitor in Cardiff or elsewhere in Wales, use the Law Society’s official 'Find a Solicitor' service. It is a free England-and-Wales directory with quick and advanced search by legal issue and location.

Compensation: Welsh NHS redress scheme under the National Health Service (Concerns, Complaints and Redress Arrangements) (Wales) Regulations. For NHS/public care in Wales, compensation can begin inside the NHS complaints process: if the Welsh NHS body investigating the concern decides a qualifying liability exists or may exist, it must consider whether to offer redress. From 1 April 2026 the amending regulations raise the redress compensation cap from £25,000 to £50,000; if the value is above that, compensation should be pursued outside the redress part of the scheme, usually by a court claim. (one official source)

Paying for help: Legal Aid / conditional fee funding in England and Wales. For an adult wrist-misdiagnosis claim like this, ordinary civil legal aid is not the main route: the clinical-negligence scope in LASPO is tightly limited to severe neurological injury caused before birth or within the short period after birth. An out-of-scope case can still seek exceptional case funding if refusing legal aid would breach human-rights-based rights, and private funding by 'no win, no fee' is allowed, with the success fee capped in personal injury claims.
The official routes are now mapped from provider, Welsh Government, ombudsman, legislation, Law Society and Llais sources, so I’m closing the plan.

Your A&E care was NHS/public care run by Cardiff and Vale University Health Board, so you start by complaining to that Health Board under Wales’ NHS complaints process. If you are not satisfied, you can go to the Public Services Ombudsman for Wales, and if compensation is in issue there is a Wales redress route inside the complaint system for lower-value cases plus the usual court claim route with a 3-year time limit. Legal aid for an adult wrist-misdiagnosis claim is usually not in scope, so most people would look at the Health Board’s redress route or a no-win-no-fee solicitor.

trace.detail:
Question: When can someone bring an NHS complaint to the Public Services Ombudsman for Wales, what must happen first, and what is the time limit? Quote the key lines and note any links to apply.
Someone can bring an NHS complaint to the Public Services Ombudsman for Wales after first taking it to the relevant local Health Board or Trust and usually after that body has responded. The page says you should complain to the Health Board or Trust promptly, and for LTP the Ombudsman can look at complaints made within one year of the matters complained about (or within one year of becoming aware of the issue); if the complaint is about something more than a year old but was raised with the Health Board or Trust in time, you should complain to the Ombudsman within 12 weeks of the response. It also says it is unlikely they will consider a complaint made before the NHS body has had up to 6 months to respond.

trace.detail:
Question: What are the rules for making an NHS complaint or concern in Wales: time limit, who to complain to first, any response times, and what happens if compensation may be due? Quote the key lines.
You can take up to 12 months to raise a concern or complaint, though it is best to do so as soon as possible. First, talk to the staff involved if you can; if not, contact the health board or trust’s complaints team, or for GP/dentist/pharmacist/optician concerns, ask the practice to look into it (you may also ask the health board or trust’s complaints team). The complaints team should respond within 30 working days, and if compensation may be due the page says to contact the Public Services Ombudsman for Wales if you are not satisfied with the response, but it does not spell out a separate compensation procedure here.

Question: What does this legislation note say about the success-fee cap in personal injury claims? Quote the key line and explain whether it applies in England and Wales.
The note says the success fee in a personal injury claim is capped at 25% of certain damages: “Article 5 provides that, in a claim for personal injuries, the success fee shall be limited to a maximum of 25%...”. trace.detail:
Question: What do these amending regulations change about the Wales NHS concerns and complaints process, especially the language or timing from 2026? Quote the key lines.
These amendments add an “early resolution period” and “early resolution procedure,” meaning concerns can be resolved before investigation, and if resolved in that period they are excluded from the later investigation/redress stages. The main timing changes are that the early resolution period is “no longer than 10 working days,” notifications to other responsible bodies become “not later than five working days,” and several later-stage deadlines are shortened or recast as “120 working days” instead of “six months” or “twelve months,” all from 1 April 2026. The amendments also change the compensation limit from £25,000 to £50,000 and require in-person communication for certain discussions and report meetings.

trace.detail:
Question: What new timing rules does this instrument set for early resolution and the overall handling of concerns from 1 April 2026? Quote the key lines.
From 1 April 2026, the new “early resolution period” is “a period of no longer than 10 working days” starting when the responsible body acknowledges receipt of the notification, and the concern must be resolved during that period before any investigation under regulation 23. The instrument also says that if early resolution succeeds, the concern is excluded from the later arrangements, while if it is not resolved the responsible body must begin investigating the concern under regulation 23. It also requires the responsible body to seek confirmation of consent before using early resolution and, after attempting it, to confirm the outcome as soon as reasonably possible.

Question: What does regulation 32 say about legal advice and medical experts for a person offered redress? Quote the key lines.
Regulation 32 says that if a Welsh NHS body has determined a qualifying liability exists or may exist, it must ensure legal advice is available to the person seeking redress, and if medical experts need to be instructed, that instruction is carried out jointly by the Welsh NHS body and the person who notified the concern. Question: What does this part of Schedule 1 say clinical negligence legal aid covers? Quote the key lines and explain whether it is limited to infants with severe neurological injury.
Clinical negligence legal aid covers "Civil legal services provided in relation to a claim for damages in respect of clinical negligence which caused a neurological injury to an individual (“V”) as a result of which V is severely disabled, but only where the first and second conditions are met." It is not limited to infants only; the text covers any individual V, though the first condition limits the negligence to when V was in the womb or during/after birth and before a specified period ends. So it is about severely disabled individuals with a neurological injury from clinical negligence, not exclusively infants with severe neurological injury.

Question: What does the Limitation Act 1980 say about the time limit for personal injury negligence claims and the date of knowledge? Quote the key lines.
For personal injury negligence claims, the Act says the claim must be brought within three years from the date the cause of action accrued or, if later, the date of knowledge of the injured person. The page also says the date of knowledge means the date when the person first knew the injury was significant, that it was attributable to the act or omission alleged, and the identity of the defendant. For these claims, knowledge of the law itself is irrelevant.

trace.detail:
Question: What exactly are the conditions in paragraph 23 for clinical-negligence legal aid? Quote the key lines showing the birth-related neurological-injury limits.
Paragraph 23 covers civil legal services for a claim for damages for clinical negligence causing a neurological injury to a severely disabled individual, but only if both the first and second conditions are met. The key birth-related limit is that the negligence must have occurred either while V was in the mother’s womb, or during or after birth but only within the specified 8-week period after the relevant birth date. The second condition is that the services are provided to V, or to V’s personal representative if V has died.
